newsitem.title: USA: Clinton sees hope for Israeli-Syria peace talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton sees hope for Israeli-Syria peace talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu exchanged ideas on Thursday on how to restart Israeli-Syrian peace talks but gave no public hint on how they planned to proceed.
During an otherwise friendly visit, a potential sale of U.S.-made F-16 jet fighters to Saudi Arabia emerged as a possible sore point between the two allies.
Israeli-Syrian negotiations have long been stuck over the fate of the strategic Golan Heights, captured by Israel in the 1967 Middle East war. Damascus wants the heights back, Israel says no.

But the parties are hoping that good will generated by a deal last month for Israel to hand over most of the West Bank town of Hebron to Palestinian rule will translate into new momentum toward peace and stability in the region.

At a White House East Room news conference with Netanyahu after their fourth meeting since the Israeli prime minister took office, Clinton said he was hopeful Israel and Syria would resume negotiations.
"I do feel encouraged by the discussions we've had that there are things worth working on, but I have nothing specific to say at this time," Clinton said.
But Netanyahu gave no indication he was prepared to soften Israel's firm position that it was not willing to give up occupation of the Golan Heights.

"No. We have a stated position," he told reporters at the Defence Department, where he met Defence Secretary William Cohen. "It is clear that we think the Golan Heights is crucial, vital territory for the defence of Israel. And that position has not changed."

"Why don't you ask it of Assad?" snapped Netanyahu in response to the question, suggesting that Syrian President Hafez al-Assad should be asked if he is willing to give up the Golan for peace with Israel.

Clinton said he would "seriously consider" any Saudi request to purchase F-16 planes, while promising not to let such a sale undermine America's commitment that Israel retain a qualitative military edge over its Arab neighbours.

The Saudis have made clear they would like F-16s to replace their 114 ageing U.S.-built F-5 fighters. Saudi Defence and Aviation Minister Prince Sultan will visit Washington in late February, but has denied reports that he might bring a formal request for the multibillion-dollar purchase of up to 100 Lockheed Martin Corp F-16s.
Netanyahu, going into a meeting with Defence Secretary William Cohen, signalled concern when asked whether he would oppose the sale.
"We're concerned about it. I am going to speak to the secretary. We will speak about it as friends with a common interest," he said.

Clinton defended Israel's troop deployment in southern Lebanon to protect its northern border from attacks against Hizbollah guerrillas. He said America had to be "somewhat deferential under these circumstances."
Netanyahu said to achieve an ultimate Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon would require a dismantlement of Hizbollah's military capacity, preferably by the Lebanese army. Syria could help, he said.
"That is something that we're prepared to negotiate with the government of Lebanon, and it's no secret with Syria, which has more than a minor influence in Lebanon," he said.

Netanyahu is the first in a parade of Middle East leaders scheduled to visit Washington over the next several weeks. He will be followed by Palestinian President Yasser Arafat, Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and King Hussein of Jordan.
